bull.b: PepGen’s proprietary EDO platform targets a meaningful technical challenge in oligonucleotide medicines: reaching relevant tissues and cells. If development succeeds, the platform could support multiple therapies across severe neuromuscular and neurological diseases rather than relying on a single product.

The Phase 2 DM1 results provide clinical validation beyond biomarker activity, with reported improvements in hand opening, grip strength, walking, and mobility tests. Strong splicing correction and favorable tolerability support continued development and may improve the program’s ability to advance toward later-stage testing.

Relatively modest leverage and declining debt reduce fixed financial obligations compared with a more highly indebted biotechnology company. This gives PepGen greater balance-sheet flexibility while its programs remain in development, even though operating losses still require substantial ongoing funding.

bear.b: PepGen has not yet established commercial revenue, so its business model currently depends on advancing clinical programs rather than recurring product sales. Until a therapy is approved and launched, the company lacks operating revenue to offset research costs or demonstrate sustainable commercial margins.

Sustained operating and free-cash-flow losses consume resources while PepGen funds clinical development and other activities. Although burn improved from approximately $81.6M in 2025, the continuing absolute outflow increases dependence on available liquidity and future financing to maintain development plans.

A partial clinical hold introduces regulatory uncertainty around the FREEDOM2 program and can complicate trial execution, timelines, or required supporting work. Even with positive clinical data, unresolved nonclinical findings could delay development and make the path to approval less predictable.
